# Development roadmap

The binary workflow now includes traced boundaries, phase-fraction gradients,
independent sample checks, Auto/Manual temperature ranges, live previews,
cancellation, inspection, and structured export. Windows sharing-lock handling
and targeted equilibrium retries are implemented. Synthetic scientific
regression tests and local Al–Cu, Ta–Zr, and Re–W browser checks cover numerical and
workflow behavior; published alloy benchmark validation remains outstanding.

The outlines below retain acceptance criteria for the broader project. They are
not all completed features. Material-point arc melting with equilibrium cooling and supplementary Kawin
tracer diffusion are implemented. Scheil solidification, precipitation kinetics,
calibrated property prediction, and optimization remain planned.
Alloy Studio can fit a preliminary flow law to a measured tensile curve.
The planned alloy-design workflow will calculate the flow curve from phase
states and processing-driven microstructure. It will use that curve to
predict yield, hardness, and UTS and account for fracture when it can limit
the tensile peak. [Mechanical properties](mechanical-properties.md)

The following are local issue outlines; no external issue tracker tickets have been created.

## 1. Database management foundation

Implementation detail: [Automatic TDB catalog and selection plan](database-selection-plan.md).

Deliver a catalog, configurable source registration, checksum-based duplicate detection, TDB parsing/validation, coverage inspection, and persistent source selection.

Acceptance:
- Register the existing database collection without editing source files.
- Distinguish thermodynamic, mobility, and volume capabilities.
- Given a requested system, explain suitable candidates and missing coverage.
- Save a selection with immutable source identity for reproducible runs.
- Report parsing failures without preventing valid files from being cataloged.

## 2. Binary phase diagram workflow

Deliver the first pycalphad adapter, explicit composition/units validation, calculation job lifecycle, structured results, plotting, and export.

Acceptance:
- Reproduce a documented reference binary diagram within stated tolerances.
- Keep numerical results and provenance independent of the displayed plot.
- Explain invalid inputs, unsupported systems, and failed calculations.
- Keep the UI responsive during a calculation and expose job status.

## 3. UI/UX foundation

The current interface has an animated intro, an interactive title screen, a tile menu, appearance settings, and the phase-diagram workspace. See the [interface guide](ui-ux.md) for screen behavior and styling.

The Alloy studio menu opens Optimize alloy with composition bounds, arc melting,
property goals/limits, and review, or Create alloy with exact composition amounts,
arc melting, and review. Both share Al/Fe/Ni families. Phase simulation uses pycalphad
initial/melt/cooling equilibria and compatible Kawin tracer diffusion, with explicit
assumptions and source transformations. Property optimization, precipitation time
integration, and persisted project browsing remain planned. See [processing](processing.md).

Acceptance:
- A user can reach a diagram without manually choosing a TDB when a verified default is available.
- Ambiguous coverage prompts an understandable choice instead of silently selecting an arbitrary source.
- Forms are keyboard accessible and display units and composition basis.
- Loading, empty, success, and failure states are implemented.

## Later milestones

1. Curated property imports, phase-aware molar volume/density, and uncertainty metadata.
2. Scheil solidification and explicit transfer to processing simulations.
3. Processing models for grain size, precipitation, and other relevant microstructure variables, with compatible thermodynamic and mobility data and experimental validation.
4. A shared constitutive flow curve for yield, hardness, and the necking-controlled tensile peak. Use measured hardness as an optional constraint with independently established hardening. Couple a fracture or damage model when premature failure can limit the peak. Validate the individual stages and the full workflow with independent benchmarks.
5. Composition/process optimization with validity constraints and uncertainty-aware comparison.
6. Additional alloy families and optional ESPEI/matminer integrations.
# Alloy processing methods

Alloy Studio calculates the equilibrium of a homogeneous material point at fixed
pressure. The starting route can include an arc melt and sampled equilibrium
cooling, or start with a solid alloy. The solver verifies a fully liquid melt
for the arc-melting route. Results report phase amounts on a molar basis and
phase compositions on an atomic basis. [Alloy studio walkthrough](../README.md#alloy-studio)

The ordered schedule supports temperature changes, anneals, quenches, and a
final cold-work thickness reduction. The editor uses °C and minutes. API inputs
use K and seconds. The temperature chart shows event order, with no time scale.
The job preserves settings for every event and calculates an independent
equilibrium at each thermal setpoint. The quenched result is the equilibrium
at the target temperature. The entered duration, hold time, quench medium, and
cold-work reduction are preserved for future kinetic and deformation models.
Cold work adds no equilibrium solve. Segregation, precipitation, quench
transformations, and grain evolution remain model gaps.

An automatic anneal could first screen the temperature interval for the
specified phase objective and incipient melting using the selected assessment.
Selecting a temperature and hold time for a target such as recrystallized
fraction or grain size requires the starting condition, kinetic parameters,
and a validated model. The Anneal event uses a user-entered setpoint and hold.
[Equilibrium phase fractions](https://pycalphad.org/docs/latest/examples/2_Computing_Properties/1_PhaseCompositions.html)
· [Recrystallization modeling](https://www.matcalc.at/images/stories/publications/phd_thesis_buken_2018.pdf)

Create alloy submits fixed additions in wt% or at%. Optimize alloy uses half
of each addition's maximum for the nominal phase simulation. The base fills the
balance. The saved `composition_mode` identifies the rule. A fixed request
supplies equal minimum and maximum values for each addition.

The default source root contains the named Al, Fe, and Ni MatCalc thermodynamic
and mobility pairs. The worker snapshots the original TDB and mobility data,
records checksums and solver versions, and writes a separate converted TDB for
pycalphad. Manual thermodynamic sources retain their own models. Kawin evaluates
tracer diffusivities where the paired mobility source and the selected phase
model are compatible. [Bundled databases and source terms](../data/matcalc/README.md)

## Plain-carbon steel equilibrium

In Alloy Studio, choose **Iron** and select **Carbon** as the sole addition.
With the default MatCalc Fe 2.062 source, **Processing → Phase selection**
defaults to **Plain-carbon steel (Fe–Fe₃C)**. Entering 0.40 wt% C in Create alloy
automatically leaves 99.60 wt% Fe. Optimize alloy retains the half-maximum rule,
so a maximum of 0.80 wt% C gives the same nominal composition.

The steel policy considers liquid, ferrite, austenite and cementite at every
stage. It suspends graphite and specialized models such as `BCC_DISL` and
`H_BCC`. This is the conventional metastable Fe–Fe₃C equilibrium used for
plain-carbon steel. The pinned MatCalc assessment represents ferrite through
the `BCC_B2` model’s linked `BCC_A2` contribution in binary Fe–C. The UI shows
the metallurgical names alongside the original solver labels. Results save the
policy, suppressed phases, solver labels, source checksum, and carbon balance.
[MatCalc’s stepped steel equilibrium example](https://www.matcalc.at/wiki/doku.php?id=tutorials:t3)

Choose **All compatible phases** for the unrestricted source calculation.
Multicomponent Iron compositions and manual sources in Studio use that policy.
Direct API requests can select `phase_policy: "fe_cementite"` for binary Fe–C
with the exact bundled assessment bytes. Requests without a policy use
`all_compatible`.

The 0.40 wt% C regression at 298.15 K and 101325 Pa checks ferrite and roughly
7.33 mol% cementite against the carbon lever rule and the Gustafson Fe–C
assessment with graphite suspended. A live check at 0.76 wt% C and 101325 Pa
found ferrite plus cementite at 990 K and austenite at 1010 K. The mode predicts
equilibrium phase assemblages. Pearlite morphology, martensite, cooling-rate
effects and steel property coverage require their own models and validation.

## Materials Project density and modulus

Processing requests default to `include_reference_properties: true`, with an
opt-out control in Processing. Create alloy and Optimize alloy's nominal phase
simulation both use the [bundled phase translation](matcalc-mp-translation-layer.md).
The exact thermodynamic source SHA-256 and phase model name select the inventory
entry. This includes all 69 deterministic mappings and 45 exact attributions.
Results record the selected crystal, decision, confidence, rationale, snapshot
checksums, and MP database version. Inventory counts describe the assessment.
Property coverage describes the molar amounts in the final equilibrium.

Each phase instance is checked against its nominal reference independently. A
maximum difference of 0.02 absolute atomic fraction per element allows transfer
of the reference atomic molar volume and elasticity as approximations. Linked
models with unresolved ordering cannot transfer translated properties. Pending
or non-crystalline entries carry no translated properties. A positive density
from the snapshot can be used offline, with supported local MatCalc DP density
taking precedence. Snapshot density reflects the recorded MP calculation.
Elasticity requires an independently validated stiffness tensor for the selected
material ID. Bundled Hill moduli alone are insufficient to validate stiffness.

A configured server-side key enables API requests after equilibrium completes.
Native process
environment values take precedence over the gitignored root `.env`, which is
loaded by `scripts/run_app.py`. Browser-session keys are forwarded only through
worker environment variables. Credentials are never stored in job JSON, source
snapshots, caches, result exports, or worker logs.

For sources outside the bundled inventory, provisional reference screening starts
with the chemical system of components above 2 at%
in each final phase. Candidates must have positive density, be nondeprecated,
match a supported prototype's space group, and differ by at most 0.02 absolute
atomic fraction for every element. Supported constraints include FCC_A1 (225),
BCC_A2 (229), HCP_A3 (194), diamond (227), and Al2Cu C16 / theta (140). The pinned
MatCalc Al, Fe, and Ni assessments also supply source-specific constraints for
FCCAL, H_BCC, Mg2Si (225), and L1₂ gamma prime (221). An explicitly linked
disordered prototype can supply a labeled surrogate with unresolved ordering.
The screening remains provisional because distinct structures can share the
same composition and space group.

Candidates are ranked by composition difference, then energy above hull. Density
uses the highest-ranked candidate. Elasticity checks up to ten ranked candidates
and can select a different material. If none has usable elasticity, a targeted
summary search filters on `has_props=elasticity` and the prototype's space group
for both the original chemical system and the full phase chemistry, including
dilute elements. The same composition and structure checks apply to up to ten
additional candidates. If the initial summary could not supply a density
reference, a successful candidate from the targeted search can supply both
properties. Truncated responses are excluded from selection. Results retain
the individual reference IDs and query payloads.

Reference atomic molar volume is calculated as reference molar mass divided by
reference density. That volume is transferred to the CALPHAD phase as an explicit
approximation. Each phase's actual molar mass uses its equilibrium composition
and TDB atomic masses. With n_i the molar phase fraction, density is
sum(n_i M_i) / sum(n_i V_i), and volume fraction is n_i V_i / sum(n_j V_j).
All phases need density coverage; missing phases are never renormalized away.

Elasticity records must be nondeprecated and have a finite symmetric positive-
definite 6×6 tensor. The raw stiffness takes precedence, with the IEEE-format
stiffness used when raw stiffness is absent. If Hill bulk or shear moduli are
missing, both are calculated from the validated tensor using pymatgen. Reported
# Rutile interface

## Implemented screens

- **Loading.** A one-second black-screen intro reveals the connected Joeltech JT monogram diagonally in Joeltech blue before fading it out. The lab-grown rutile then spins and zooms in, with prismatic rays around the crystal and the white Rutile title appearing over it. There is no Skip intro button; reduced motion bypasses the intro.
- **Title.** Use **Start** or press a character key, Enter, or Space to open the main menu. The gem responds to dragging and arrow keys, with no hint on the title screen. Vertical drag and arrow controls follow the requested direction; the controls also work on the main menu backdrop. Settings is also available here. The JT monogram appears during the loading sequence.
- **Main menu.** The camera changes angle and approaches the same crystal until its facets fill the backdrop. The crystal turns very slowly while the menu is idle. The glass tiles open **Generate phase diagrams**, **Alloy studio**, and **Settings**. One disabled **Under construction** tile reserves space for future materials workflows.
- **Alloy studio.** The second menu tile opens a submenu with **Optimize alloy**, **Create alloy**, and **Mechanical properties**. Optimize alloy opens a five-step setup preview: alloy family, composition, processing, goals and limits, and review. Create alloy shares the same families and processing controls, but uses exact addition amounts, automatically assigns the remainder to the base metal, and skips goals and limits in navigation and review. Composition places the element picker beside the amount editor on desktop. A proportional bar and a labeled balance update as exact additions change. Both paths retain wt%/at% basis selection without implicit conversion. Step changes return to the top with focus on the step heading so the shell Back button stays available; there is no intro badge or duplicate progress row. The family aside names the source; assessment limitations remain in source help and review. The shared crystal zoom introduces the page. A large tile grid shows Mg, Al, Ti, Fe, Ni, Co, Cu, Zn, Zr, Ag, W, Pt, Au, and Pb in increasing atomic-weight order, followed by an Other tile with a + symbol. Ni precedes Co by atomic weight. The compact family buttons use beveled square symbols with glass lighting. Al, Fe, and Ni glow and have available setup previews; other families and Other are gray and disabled. Fe has a subtle red tint and Ni a subtle green tint. The grid reflows without horizontal scrolling on mobile. MatCalc sources and named mobility companions ship in the data folder and are available to the processing simulation by default; their assessment coverage is not automatically established. The optimizer entry retains the shared crystal zoom but never draws the Ti/O lattice. No atoms appear before family selection. Selecting Al lights up the atoms in a fixed FCC aluminum reference lattice one by one (instant with reduced motion) with nearest-neighbor links, using the same depth-layer renderer and settled high-DPI cache as the rutile scene. The conventional cell has corner and face-center sites. Its spacing and orientation are for display; it does not represent a calculated alloy state, and adding elements does not relabel the FCC Al sites. Opening Composition widens the workspace on desktop. The lattice smoothly magnifies by 30% as it dims to 16% opacity. Later steps retain this view; returning to the family step restores the original framing. Reduced motion applies the framing immediately, and magnified caches retain native pixel density. Leaving the optimizer preserves the selected reference lattice during the return transition.
- **Settings background.** The camera accelerates into a facet as the TiO₂ lattice comes into view. The two scenes overlap during the dive. The lens widens during the move and eases into the final field of view. Near, middle, and far atoms scale at different rates to give the lattice depth. The close framing shows fewer atoms, with space between the red O and blue Ti spheres. Each sphere has a luminous rim, soft bloom, and reflections tinted by nearby bonded neighbours. The lattice holds its orientation after the camera arrives, and atoms and bonds fade into black at the sides and in the distance. The browser caches each depth layer beyond the viewport at its widest point and renders the gem at a lower resolution during the move. When the GPU is busy, the next frame uses the current camera pose and draws the gem and lattice together. The scene uses a repeated tetragonal unit cell and simplified bonds. [Rutile crystallographic coordinates](https://github.com/cryos/avogadro/blob/master/crystals/oxides/TiO2-Rutile.cif)
- **Settings.** Natural rutile is the default: a single irregular, oblong red crystal with steady reflections and no prismatic rays. The selection applies when returning to the title or menu and on subsequent launches at the same app address. **Reduce motion** also persists there and skips the logo intro, holds the camera still, and suppresses rays and transitions. The app honors the operating system’s reduced-motion preference.
- **Materials Project settings.** Settings includes a password field, Save key, Clear session key, and a status identifying session or server environment configuration. A saved session key stays in server memory until restart, overrides any environment key, and is cleared from the field after submission. It is never saved in browser storage or run files. Clearing it restores any environment key. Failed saves keep the previous configuration and show an error. Key format is checked at save; authentication occurs during reference lookup. Appearance and integration controls sit side by side on desktop and stack on narrow screens.
- **Phase diagrams.** The shared entry zoom moves into the crystal and settles onto black, without a Ti/O lattice. The desktop workspace uses a compact header and the full window width. The center plot fits the available viewport height on typical desktop displays, and completed sidebars end after their content. Start with the setup panel filling the workspace: upload one thermodynamic file and choose two elements. Temperature in K, pressure in Pa, quality, and boundary tolerance are under **Calculation settings**, with Detailed selected by default. Creating a diagram reveals a second panel from the right, splitting the full workspace equally. It reports the current stage, boundary point count or independent check rows, and elapsed time. Continuation has indeterminate progress; mapping batches and checks report counted progress. There is no pulsing calculation banner. Real partial boundaries and completed sample rows appear as they become available, labeled as an incomplete preview. On completion the panel becomes the diagram and the inspector enters on the right. Narrow screens stack the panels, and reduced motion suppresses transitions. Cancellation or failure preserves an explicitly incomplete preview without enabling export. The workspace keeps job state when returning to the menu.
- **Diagram inspection.** Solids use vibrant colors and liquid is always black; mixed fields blend by molar phase amounts. Phase labels use compact text with a contrast halo. Labels fit inside their phase field where possible. Narrow fields use short nearby leaders with anchor dots, with the right margin available for labels that cannot fit locally. Drag a label to move it; keyboard focus plus arrow keys moves it too, with Shift for larger steps. The anchor remains fixed at its phase location. Reset label positions restores automatic placement. Positions last for the current run and do not change exported scientific data. Red crosses identify independent sample disagreements outside the boundary tolerance (0.25% of axis span by default). Ignored differences remain inspectable. Calculation conditions, check counts, sample overlay, warnings and provenance sit below System setup. Independent checks and warnings keep their summaries visible when collapsed. Phase colors sits below the inspector and opens to beveled chips with contrasting text. New uploads clear the previous result and legend; previews display only their current phases while retaining assigned colors within a run. The sample overlay, keyboard inspection, and textual check summary provide alternatives to color alone. Hover or tap to inspect, use arrow keys to move when the plot has focus, and Enter or Escape to pin or unpin. The inspector leads with the selected structures and point coordinates. It uses conventional FCC, BCC and HCP names and documented prototypes for the bundled examples. Other phases retain their assessment names. Phase cards show amounts in mol% and compositions in at%. Expand the point details to see the calculation source, nearest sample and comparisons. The tracking marker fades over labels and reappears at the new pointer location when inspection resumes. The pinned marker and Unpin button fade during a label drag and return to the pinned point. JSON exports preserve boundaries, checks, settings, warnings, and provenance.

Use **Back** to move from a submenu to its entry screen. Escape also goes back when focus is outside form fields and the plot. The menu and workspace reflow on narrow screens.

New subpages must retain the shared crystal-to-lattice zoom and delayed content
entrance. Use a `.screen` section with `id="screen-<name>"` and a matching
`data-open="<name>"` menu button. The scene automatically applies the dive to
screens beyond loading, title, and menu; the generic `[data-dive] .screen` rule
synchronizes their content. Reduced motion continues to bypass the animation.

Workspace panels share three interpolated grid tracks, so the existing panel
contracts smoothly as space opens for another panel. The new panel unfolds from
its upper-left corner. The submenu lens widening and lattice zoom are more
pronounced; both still settle into a stationary view and honor reduced motion.
The wide lattice cache is used only during the dive. On arrival, visible layers
are rebuilt at the settled view's pixel density, with a separate 24-million-pixel
budget across the three layers, so the stronger FOV does not blur the resting view.

Generation steps occupy the full row at equal widths. Their backgrounds fill
using reported work counts: 22 melting-probe steps (10 brackets, 10 refinements, hull screening, and confirmation), four equilibrium edge searches, batches within each adaptive
mapping pass, and independent samples. Mapping-pass counts reset for each pass;
they are not an estimated percentage of the entire adaptive calculation. Boundary
continuation has no known total and uses an indeterminate fill. Counts are also
included in accessible labels. Finished stages remain filled. The inspector shows
an independent-check badge only for disagreement; nearest-sample values and
source information remain available for all points.

The temperature control defaults to **Auto · melting range + 30 K**. Manual
temperature inputs are hidden and disabled until **Manual limits** is selected;
their values are preserved when switching modes. Auto adds a **Find melting
range** step before boundary tracing. Placeholder request limits are not drawn
during estimation. Previews use the resolved limits, and the final range remains
visible beside the plot. Files without usable liquid coverage report an explicit
failure with guidance to choose Manual. Cancellation works during this preflight.

## Visual design

Use black backgrounds, mostly grayscale surfaces, white type, and JoelTech blue `#0A3D62` for selected controls and primary actions. The glass controls blur the scene behind them and add reflective rims and a soft bloom. Rim highlights follow the pointer where motion is enabled. The frost and edge lighting take cues from iPhone Liquid Glass and Windows Vista and 7. The Wii U reference informs the rounded tile menu. Keep headings and labels short, with supporting text where a control or scientific result needs explanation. [Apple’s Liquid Glass design overview](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2025/219/)

Use Momo Trust Display for titles and accents and Estedad for body, control, and plot text. Both fonts ship locally under the SIL Open Font License. [Momo Trust Display](https://github.com/typeassociates/MomoTrustDisplay) · [Estedad](https://github.com/aminabedi68/Estedad)

The lab-grown gem uses a round brilliant cut with a table, crown, girdle, pavilion, and culet. The natural specimen uses irregular red crystal faces with procedural surface texture and wavelength-dependent absorption. These are artistic effects rather than measured material properties. The WebGL renderer uses virtual studio lights and traces internal reflections and refraction through the gem facets. The Canvas fallback uses the same geometry with simpler lighting. Both scenes support pointer and keyboard rotation and pause when the tab is hidden. The scene runs in native JavaScript without downloaded artwork or a graphics library. [GIA round brilliant anatomy](https://4cs.gia.edu/en-us/diamond-cut/)

## Alloy Studio setup and simulation

The current wizard preserves selections while the app tab remains open, including
when returning to the menu. Next and the top navigation share live validation; changing inputs immediately updates reachable steps and disables invalid forward navigation. Removing a required element or entering invalid processing temperatures revokes access to downstream steps. Previous, the shell
Back control, and Escape outside form fields return to the previous step. Back
from the family step returns to the menu. Completed steps and review Edit controls
allow changes; forward jumps recheck intervening steps. There is no persisted
project or optimization job yet.

Composition bounds use explicitly selected mass or atomic percent. Changing basis
reinterprets the numbers without converting them, as stated beside the controls.
Al, Fe, and Ni families are selectable, with MatCalc thermodynamic sources
bundled for the arc-melting simulation with their named mobility companions attached by default. The selected base is the composition balance
and is excluded from addition options; maximum additions must leave a positive balance.
Fe uses a subtly red BCC reference background; Ni uses a subtly green FCC
background, and Al retains blue FCC. These are illustrative reference lattices,
not predicted phases at the entered processing conditions. Addition options are setup choices, not verified interaction coverage.
Processing puts a setpoint chart next to a compact event list on desktop and
above it on mobile. Choose arc melt and cool, or start from a solid alloy. Add a
temperature change, anneal, quench with a selected medium, or cold work with a
thickness reduction. Thermal events can be reordered, and cold work stays at
the end. The chart uses °C and event order. Source, pressure, and property
reference controls are under **Source & calculation settings**.
For Iron with carbon as the sole addition and the default MatCalc Fe source,
**Phase selection** defaults to **Plain-carbon steel (Fe–Fe₃C)**. The user can
select **All compatible phases**. Review shows the selected policy, and the
steel result labels ferrite, austenite and cementite alongside their solver names.
Create alloy reviews the exact composition entered. Optimize alloy reviews a
nominal composition at half of each maximum addition, with the base as balance.
The final phase table uses
molar amounts and atomic compositions. Expandable details contain initial/melt
states, the sampled cooling path, Kawin diffusion context, assumptions, and sources.
Ordered models identify their linked disordered states beside the phase label.
**Simulate phases** is the fourth Review card. It opens a separate Results step
after the job completes. Runs have counted progress, cancellation, JSON export,
and explicit failures. Editing the setup marks the previous result as belonging
to the submitted settings.
Results includes a schematic microstructure viewer with scroll
and keyboard zoom, drag and keyboard panning, and adjustable illustrative grain
size and layers. Results use the equilibrium phase identities and display their
molar amounts in the legend. Grain geometry, colored area, spinodal patterns,
and precipitate layers are illustrative.
See [processing methods](processing.md).

Goals specify maximize/minimize; property limits specify upper/lower bounds with
units. Yield strength, density, fracture toughness, and Young's modulus are
selectable requirements, all labeled as needing models/data. Repeated goals and
contradictory limits are rejected. The review preserves processing inputs and explains missing property integrations.
**Simulate phases** runs the equilibrium calculation and evaluates enabled
density and elasticity methods. Goals and limits are stored as setup inputs.
Property optimization remains planned.

When an ingot-based alloy-design sequence is implemented, its camera can pull back
to reveal an ingot and introduce the actual processing steps. The current setup
uses the shared zoom on entry and quieter content transitions between steps. Keep

"""Explicit MatCalc family companions; no ranking or assessment concatenation."""
from pathlib import Path
import os
import re

from rutile3.data.catalog import checksum


FAMILY_SOURCES = {
    "AL": ("mc_al_v2037.tdb", "mc_al_v2008.ddb"),
    "FE": ("mc_fe_v2062.tdb", "mc_fe_v2016.ddb"),
    "NI": ("mc_ni_v2036.tdb", "mc_ni_v2012.ddb"),
}
# Declared element sets for these exact versions, used if external files are
# unavailable. When available, read the ELEMENT declarations from the source.
FAMILY_ELEMENTS = {
    "AL": "AL CR CU FE MG MN NI SC SI TI ZN ZR".split(),
    "FE": "AL B C CO CR CU FE H HF LA MN MO N NB NI O P PD S SI TA TI V W Y".split(),
    "NI": "AL B C CO CR CU FE HF LA MN MO N NB NI O S SI TI V W Y ZR".split(),
}
# The steel phase policy was checked against these exact MatCalc Fe 2.062 bytes.
STEEL_SOURCE_SHA256 = "aa02077eac3f602dd7479cbeafb09b450e282716752b3ae2b1fc3a57d9c64865"


def validate_phase_policy_source(request, source_sha256):
    if request.phase_policy == "fe_cementite" and source_sha256 != STEEL_SOURCE_SHA256:
        raise ValueError("Fe–Fe₃C equilibrium requires the bundled MatCalc Fe 2.062 assessment.")


def declared_elements(raw):
    content = raw.decode("utf-8-sig", errors="replace")
    content = "\n".join(line.split("$")[0] for line in content.splitlines())
    return sorted(set(re.findall(r"(?im)^\s*ELEMENT\s+([A-Z]{1,2})\s", content)) - {"VA"})


def find_companion(root, filename):
    # Restrict to the named companion; never silently use an older assessment.
    matches = sorted(Path(root).rglob(filename)) if Path(root).is_dir() else []
    if not matches:
        return None
    contents = {checksum(path.read_bytes()) for path in matches}
    if len(contents) != 1:
        raise ValueError(f"Multiple different {filename} files exist. Import a specific TDB instead.")
    return matches[0]


def sources(root):
    result = []
    for family, (thermodynamic, mobility) in FAMILY_SOURCES.items():
        path = find_companion(root, thermodynamic)
        diffusion = find_companion(root, mobility)
        raw = path.read_bytes() if path else None
        result.append({"family": family, "thermodynamic": thermodynamic, "mobility": mobility,
                       "available": path is not None, "mobility_available": diffusion is not None,
                       "elements": declared_elements(raw) if raw is not None else FAMILY_ELEMENTS[family],
                       "steel_equilibrium_available": family == "FE" and raw is not None and checksum(raw) == STEEL_SOURCE_SHA256,
                       "element_list_source": "source declarations" if path else "version manifest; source unavailable",
                       "assessment_coverage": "unverified"})
    return result


def resolve_sources(catalog, request):
    if request.database_id:
        metadata = catalog.inspect(request.database_id)
        path, raw = catalog.verified_source(metadata)
        # A manually selected assessment is not automatically compatible with
        # the MatCalc companion, even if phase names happen to match.
        return path, raw, None
    thermodynamic, mobility = FAMILY_SOURCES[request.family]
    path = find_companion(catalog.source_root, thermodynamic)
    if path is None:
        raise ValueError(f"{thermodynamic} is unavailable. Import a thermodynamic TDB or configure RUTILE_DATABASE_ROOT.")
    diffusion = find_companion(catalog.source_root, mobility)
    companion = None if diffusion is None else {"name": diffusion.name, "raw": diffusion.read_bytes()}
    return path, path.read_bytes(), companion


def physical_source(catalog):
    configured = os.environ.get("RUTILE_PHYSICAL_DATABASE")
    path = Path(configured) if configured else find_companion(catalog.source_root, "physical_data.pdb")
    if path is None or not path.is_file():
        return None
    description = path.parent / "DESCRIPTION.md"
    return {"name": path.name, "raw": path.read_bytes(), "path": str(path.resolve()),
            "description": description.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if description.exists() else None}

# Bundled MatCalc open databases

These are unmodified copies of the MatCalc basic open databases by Erwin
Povoden-Karadeniz (TU Wien), with additional authors and literature credited in
the original files. They are included so a repository download can run the
Al, Fe, and Ni family workflows without a separate database download.

| Family | Thermodynamic assessment | Automatically attached mobility |
|---|---|---|
| Al | `al/mc_al_v2037.tdb` (2.037) | `al/mc_al_v2008.ddb` (2.008) |
| Fe | `fe/mc_fe_v2062.tdb` (2.062) | `fe/mc_fe_v2016.ddb` (2.016) |
| Ni | `ni/mc_ni_v2036.tdb` (2.036) | `ni/mc_ni_v2012.ddb` (2.012) |

`physical/physical_data.pdb` (1.03) provides the optional local density parameters.
Its collection description is preserved beside it. The database files retain
their original bytes, encodings, line endings, notices, and references.
[manifest.json](manifest.json) records the original collection paths, roles,
versions, byte sizes, SHA-256 checksums, and absence of transformations. Some
upstream license comments retain older version numbers; those comments have
been preserved.

Source and compatibility information:
[MatCalc open databases](https://www.matcalc.at/index.php/databases/open-databases).
The publisher lists Fe mobility 2.016 for Fe thermodynamics 2.062 or newer,
Ni mobility 2.012 for Ni thermodynamics 2.036 or newer, and Al mobility 2.008
for Al thermodynamics 2.032 or newer. These named pairs are selected explicitly;
assessments are not concatenated. Arbitrary manually imported TDBs do not receive
a mobility companion automatically.

## Attribution and redistribution

The databases are made available under the
[Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/).
Individual contents are licensed under the
[Database Contents License (DbCL) 1.0](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/dbcl/1-0/).
These terms apply to the databases in this directory, including the physical
database as stated on the publisher's source page. Preserve the attribution,
license links, and original notices when redistributing these files. The
application's code and other datasets retain their own terms.

Original sources remain unchanged. Rutile converts supported MatCalc syntax
only in saved calculation runs, preserving source snapshots and recording
transformations and checksums. No scientific parameters are intentionally changed
in this distribution. Availability and named pairing do not establish assessed
interaction coverage, validity over arbitrary compositions or temperatures, or
experimental accuracy. Unsupported models and missing properties remain explicit.

## Source selection

This directory is the default `RUTILE_DATABASE_ROOT`. An explicit environment
override replaces it; it is not combined with a different source collection.
`RUTILE_PHYSICAL_DATABASE` can override the density file separately. Local
datasets outside this curated bundle remain ignored by version control.

Optimize alloy opens a five-step setup preview: alloy family, composition, processing, goals and limits, and review. A large tile grid shows Mg, Al, Ti, Fe, Ni, Co, Cu, Zn, Zr, Ag, W, Pt, Au, and Pb in increasing atomic-weight order, followed by an Other tile with a + symbol. Ni precedes Co by atomic weight. The compact family buttons use beveled square symbols with glass lighting. Al, Fe, and Ni glow and have available setup previews; other families and Other are gray and disabled. Fe has a subtle red tint and Ni a subtle green tint. The grid reflows without horizontal scrolling on mobile. MatCalc sources and named mobility companions ship in the data folder and are available to the processing simulation by default; their assessment coverage is not automatically established. The optimizer entry retains the shared crystal zoom but never draws the Ti/O lattice. No atoms appear before family selection. Selecting Al lights up the atoms in a fixed FCC aluminum reference lattice one by one (instant with reduced motion) with nearest-neighbor links, using the same depth-layer renderer and settled high-DPI cache as the rutile scene. The conventional cell has corner and face-center sites. Its spacing and orientation are for display; it does not represent a calculated alloy state, and adding elements does not relabel the FCC Al sites. Opening Composition widens the workspace on desktop. The lattice smoothly magnifies by 30% as it dims to 16% opacity. Later steps retain this view; returning to the family step restores the original framing. Reduced motion applies the framing immediately, and magnified caches retain native pixel density. Leaving the optimizer preserves the selected reference lattice during the return transition.

# Alloy processing methods

Alloy Studio calculates the equilibrium of a homogeneous material point at fixed
pressure. The starting route can include an arc melt and sampled equilibrium
cooling, or start with a solid alloy. The solver verifies a fully liquid melt
for the arc-melting route. Results report phase amounts on a molar basis and
phase compositions on an atomic basis. [Alloy studio walkthrough](../README.md#alloy-studio)

The ordered schedule supports temperature changes, anneals, quenches, and a
final cold-work thickness reduction. The editor uses °C and minutes. API inputs
use K and seconds. The temperature chart shows event order, with no time scale.
The job preserves settings for every event and calculates an independent
equilibrium at each thermal setpoint. The quenched result is the equilibrium
at the target temperature. The entered duration, hold time, quench medium, and
cold-work reduction are preserved for future kinetic and deformation models.
Cold work adds no equilibrium solve. Segregation, precipitation, quench
transformations, and grain evolution remain model gaps.

An automatic anneal could first screen the temperature interval for the
specified phase objective and incipient melting using the selected assessment.
Selecting a temperature and hold time for a target such as recrystallized
fraction or grain size requires the starting condition, kinetic parameters,
and a validated model. The Anneal event uses a user-entered setpoint and hold.
[Equilibrium phase fractions](https://pycalphad.org/docs/latest/examples/2_Computing_Properties/1_PhaseCompositions.html)
· [Recrystallization modeling](https://www.matcalc.at/images/stories/publications/phd_thesis_buken_2018.pdf)

Create alloy submits fixed additions in wt% or at%. Optimize alloy uses half
of each addition's maximum for the nominal phase simulation. The base fills the
balance. The saved `composition_mode` identifies the rule. A fixed request
supplies equal minimum and maximum values for each addition.

The default source root contains the named Al, Fe, and Ni MatCalc thermodynamic
and mobility pairs. The worker snapshots the original TDB and mobility data,
records checksums and solver versions, and writes a separate converted TDB for
pycalphad. Manual thermodynamic sources retain their own models. Kawin evaluates
tracer diffusivities where the paired mobility source and the selected phase
model are compatible. [Bundled databases and source terms](../data/matcalc/README.md)

## Plain-carbon steel equilibrium

In Alloy Studio, choose **Iron** and select **Carbon** as the sole addition.
With the default MatCalc Fe 2.062 source, **Processing → Phase selection**
defaults to **Plain-carbon steel (Fe–Fe₃C)**. Entering 0.40 wt% C in Create alloy
automatically leaves 99.60 wt% Fe. Optimize alloy retains the half-maximum rule,
so a maximum of 0.80 wt% C gives the same nominal composition.

The steel policy considers liquid, ferrite, austenite and cementite at every
stage. It suspends graphite and specialized models such as `BCC_DISL` and
`H_BCC`. This is the conventional metastable Fe–Fe₃C equilibrium used for
plain-carbon steel. The pinned MatCalc assessment represents ferrite through
the `BCC_B2` model’s linked `BCC_A2` contribution in binary Fe–C. The UI shows
the metallurgical names alongside the original solver labels. Results save the
policy, suppressed phases, solver labels, source checksum, and carbon balance.
[MatCalc’s stepped steel equilibrium example](https://www.matcalc.at/wiki/doku.php?id=tutorials:t3)

Choose **All compatible phases** for the unrestricted source calculation.
Multicomponent Iron compositions and manual sources in Studio use that policy.
Direct API requests can select `phase_policy: "fe_cementite"` for binary Fe–C
with the exact bundled assessment bytes. Requests without a policy use
`all_compatible`.
calculate proof stress and UTS and fit a flow law from an uploaded CSV or a
local reference specimen. The planned alloy-design workflow will predict
properties from calculated phases and processing-driven microstructure.
[Mechanical properties and model requirements](docs/mechanical-properties.md)

1. Open **Alloy studio → Create alloy** and select an aluminum, iron, or nickel
   family. Choose mass percent (wt%) or atomic percent (at%) and enter the amount
   of each addition. Rutile assigns the remainder to the base metal.
2. In **Processing**, choose a starting route and use **Add event** to enter
   temperature changes, anneals, quenches, or a final cold-work reduction.
   The bundled MatCalc thermodynamic assessment and its matching mobility file
   load by default.
3. In **Review**, select **Simulate phases**. **Results** shows equilibrium
   states, tracer diffusivity where supported, and a schematic colored by the
   final equilibrium phases.
   **Export phase JSON** saves the schedule, result, and source provenance.

**Optimize alloy** records composition bounds, goals, and limits. Its
**Simulate phases** action evaluates a nominal composition using half of each
maximum addition. The goals and limits are setup inputs for the planned
optimization workflow.

The solver evaluates equilibrium at the thermal setpoints. For arc melting, it
also checks for a fully liquid melt and samples equilibrium during cooling.
Quench kinetics, annealing kinetics, and deformation effects require additional
models.
[Processing methods and limits](docs/processing.md)

For plain-carbon steel, choose **Iron**, select **Carbon** alone, and use the
default **Plain-carbon steel (Fe–Fe₃C)** phase selection in Processing. Try
0.40 wt% C in Create alloy. The balance is 99.60 wt% Fe.
[Steel phase selection and limits](docs/processing.md#plain-carbon-steel-equilibrium)

### Bundled databases

The repository includes the Al, Fe, and Ni MatCalc thermodynamic assessments,

Alloy Studio calculates the equilibrium of a homogeneous material point at fixed
pressure. The starting route can include an arc melt and sampled equilibrium
cooling, or start with a solid alloy. The solver verifies a fully liquid melt
for the arc-melting route. Results report phase amounts on a molar basis and
phase compositions on an atomic basis. [Alloy studio walkthrough](../README.md#alloy-studio)

final cold-work thickness reduction. The editor uses °C and minutes. API inputs
use K and seconds. The temperature chart shows event order, with no time scale.

# Rutile interface

## Implemented screens

- **Loading.** A one-second black-screen intro reveals the connected Joeltech JT monogram diagonally in Joeltech blue before fading it out. The lab-grown rutile then spins and zooms in, with prismatic rays around the crystal and the white Rutile title appearing over it. There is no Skip intro button; reduced motion bypasses the intro.
- **Title.** Use **Start** or press a character key, Enter, or Space to open the main menu. The gem responds to dragging and arrow keys, with no hint on the title screen. Vertical drag and arrow controls follow the requested direction; the controls also work on the main menu backdrop. Settings is also available here. The JT monogram appears during the loading sequence.
- **Main menu.** The camera changes angle and approaches the same crystal until its facets fill the backdrop. The crystal turns very slowly while the menu is idle. The glass tiles open **Generate phase diagrams**, **Alloy studio**, and **Settings**. One disabled **Under construction** tile reserves space for future materials workflows.
- **Alloy studio.** The second menu tile opens a submenu with **Optimize alloy**, **Create alloy**, and **Mechanical properties**. Optimize alloy opens a five-step setup preview: alloy family, composition, processing, goals and limits, and review. Create alloy shares the same families and processing controls, but uses exact addition amounts, automatically assigns the remainder to the base metal, and skips goals and limits in navigation and review. Composition places the element picker beside the amount editor on desktop. A proportional bar and a labeled balance update as exact additions change. Both paths retain wt%/at% basis selection without implicit conversion. Step changes return to the top with focus on the step heading so the shell Back button stays available; there is no intro badge or duplicate progress row. The family aside names the source; assessment limitations remain in source help and review. The shared crystal zoom introduces the page. A large tile grid shows Mg, Al, Ti, Fe, Ni, Co, Cu, Zn, Zr, Ag, W, Pt, Au, and Pb in increasing atomic-weight order, followed by an Other tile with a + symbol. Ni precedes Co by atomic weight. The compact family buttons use beveled square symbols with glass lighting. Al, Fe, and Ni glow and have available setup previews; other families and Other are gray and disabled. Fe has a subtle red tint and Ni a subtle green tint. The grid reflows without horizontal scrolling on mobile. MatCalc sources and named mobility companions ship in the data folder and are available to the processing simulation by default; their assessment coverage is not automatically established. The optimizer entry retains the shared crystal zoom but never draws the Ti/O lattice. No atoms appear before family selection. Selecting Al lights up the atoms in a fixed FCC aluminum reference lattice one by one (instant with reduced motion) with nearest-neighbor links, using the same depth-layer renderer and settled high-DPI cache as the rutile scene. The conventional cell has corner and face-center sites. Its spacing and orientation are for display; it does not represent a calculated alloy state, and adding elements does not relabel the FCC Al sites. Opening Composition widens the workspace on desktop. The lattice smoothly magnifies by 30% as it dims to 16% opacity. Later steps retain this view; returning to the family step restores the original framing. Reduced motion applies the framing immediately, and magnified caches retain native pixel density. Leaving the optimizer preserves the selected reference lattice during the return transition.
- **Settings background.** The camera accelerates into a facet as the TiO₂ lattice comes into view. The two scenes overlap during the dive. The lens widens during the move and eases into the final field of view. Near, middle, and far atoms scale at different rates to give the lattice depth. The close framing shows fewer atoms, with space between the red O and blue Ti spheres. Each sphere has a luminous rim, soft bloom, and reflections tinted by nearby bonded neighbours. The lattice holds its orientation after the camera arrives, and atoms and bonds fade into black at the sides and in the distance. The browser caches each depth layer beyond the viewport at its widest point and renders the gem at a lower resolution during the move. When the GPU is busy, the next frame uses the current camera pose and draws the gem and lattice together. The scene uses a repeated tetragonal unit cell and simplified bonds. [Rutile crystallographic coordinates](https://github.com/cryos/avogadro/blob/master/crystals/oxides/TiO2-Rutile.cif)
- **Settings.** Natural rutile is the default: a single irregular, oblong red crystal with steady reflections and no prismatic rays. The selection applies when returning to the title or menu and on subsequent launches at the same app address. **Reduce motion** also persists there and skips the logo intro, holds the camera still, and suppresses rays and transitions. The app honors the operating system’s reduced-motion preference.

The JT monogram appears during the loading sequence.
- **Main menu.** The camera changes angle and approaches the same crystal until its facets fill the backdrop. The crystal turns very slowly while the menu is idle. The glass tiles open **Generate phase diagrams**, **Alloy studio**, and **Settings**. One disabled **Under construction** tile reserves space for future materials workflows.
- **Alloy studio.** The second menu tile opens a submenu with **Optimize alloy**, **Create alloy**, and **Mechanical properties**. Optimize alloy opens a five-step setup preview: alloy family, composition, processing, goals and limits, and review. Create alloy shares the same families and processing controls, but uses exact addition amounts, automatically assigns the remainder to the base metal, and skips goals and limits in navigation and review. Composition places the element picker beside the amount editor on desktop. A proportional bar and a labeled balance update as exact additions change. Both paths retain wt%/at% basis selection without implicit conversion. Step changes return to the top with focus on the step heading so the shell Back button stays available; there is no intro badge or duplicate progress row. The family aside names the source; assessment limitations remain in source help and review. The shared crystal zoom introduces the page. A large tile grid shows Mg, Al, Ti, Fe, Ni, Co, Cu, Zn, Zr, Ag, W, Pt, Au, and Pb in increasing atomic-weight order, followed by an Other tile with a + symbol. Ni precedes Co by atomic weight. The compact family buttons use beveled square symbols with glass lighting. Al, Fe, and Ni glow and have available setup previews; other families and Other are gray and disabled. Fe has a subtle red tint and Ni a subtle green tint. The grid reflows without horizontal scrolling on mobile. MatCalc sources and named mobility companions ship in the data folder and are available to the processing simulation by default; their assessment coverage is not automatically established. The optimizer entry retains the shared crystal zoom but never draws the Ti/O lattice. No atoms appear before family selection. Selecting Al lights up the atoms in a fixed FCC aluminum reference lattice one by one (instant with reduced motion) with nearest-neighbor links, using the same depth-layer renderer and settled high-DPI cache as the rutile scene. The conventional cell has corner and face-center sites. Its spacing and orientation are for display; it does not represent a calculated alloy state, and adding elements does not relabel the FCC Al sites. Opening Composition widens the workspace on desktop. The lattice smoothly magnifies by 30% as it dims to 16% opacity. Later steps retain this view; returning to the family step restores the original framing. Reduced motion applies the framing immediately, and magnified caches retain native pixel density. Leaving the optimizer preserves the selected reference lattice during the return transition.
- **Settings background.** The camera accelerates into a facet as the TiO₂ lattice comes into view. The two scenes overlap during the dive. The lens widens during the move and eases into the final field of view. Near, middle, and far atoms scale at different rates to give the lattice depth. The close framing shows fewer atoms, with space between the red O and blue Ti spheres. Each sphere has a luminous rim, soft bloom, and reflections tinted by nearby bonded neighbours. The lattice holds its orientation after the camera arrives, and atoms and bonds fade into black at the sides and in the distance. The browser caches each depth layer beyond the viewport at its widest point and renders the gem at a lower resolution during the move. When the GPU is busy, the next frame uses the current camera pose and draws the gem and lattice together. The scene uses a repeated tetragonal unit cell and simplified bonds. [Rutile crystallographic coordinates](https://github.com/cryos/avogadro/blob/master/crystals/oxides/TiO2-Rutile.cif)
- **Settings.** Natural rutile is the default: a single irregular, oblong red crystal with steady reflections and no prismatic rays. The selection applies when returning to the title or menu and on subsequent launches at the same app address. **Reduce motion** also persists there and skips the logo intro, holds the camera still, and suppresses rays and transitions. The app honors the operating system’s reduced-motion preference.

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

import rutile3.api.app as module
from rutile3.data.catalog import Catalog
from test_diagrams import REGULAR_SOLUTION


@pytest.fixture
def client(monkeypatch, tmp_path):
    import rutile3.data.catalog as source
    monkeypatch.setattr(source, "SOURCE_ROOT", tmp_path / "sources")
    monkeypatch.setattr(source, "WORKSPACE", tmp_path)
    monkeypatch.setattr(module, "catalog", Catalog(database_path=tmp_path / "catalog.sqlite3"))
    monkeypatch.setattr(module, "session_key", None)
    monkeypatch.delenv("MP_API_KEY", raising=False)
    with TestClient(module.app) as test_client:
        yield test_client


def test_upload_inspect_and_reject_invalid_system(client):
    response = client.post("/api/databases", json={"filename": "regular.tbd", "content": REGULAR_SOLUTION})
    assert response.status_code == 200
    metadata = response.json()
    assert metadata["elements"] == ["AL", "CU"]
    assert metadata["has_gibbs_energy"]
    assert client.get(f"/api/databases/{metadata['id']}").json()["sha256"] == metadata["sha256"]
    response = client.post("/api/diagrams", json={"database_id": metadata["id"], "components": ["AL", "ZN"]})
    assert response.status_code == 422


def test_source_without_gibbs_energy(client):
    content = REGULAR_SOLUTION.replace("PARAMETER G(", "PARAMETER V0(")
    response = client.post("/api/databases", json={"filename": "volume.tdb", "content": content})
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert not response.json()["has_gibbs_energy"]
    assert client.post("/api/diagrams", json={"database_id": response.json()["id"], "components": ["AL", "CU"]}).status_code == 422


def test_auto_temperature_defers_placeholder_range_check_to_worker(client, monkeypatch):
    metadata = client.post("/api/databases", json={"filename": "regular.tdb", "content": REGULAR_SOLUTION}).json()
    key = metadata["id"]
    response = client.put(f"/api/databases/{key}/coverage", json={
        "components": ["AL", "CU"], "assessment": "assessed", "reference": "Synthetic fixture only",
        "temperature_k": [500, 1100]})
    assert response.status_code == 200
    def start(path, settings, decision, *, snapshot):
        assert settings["temperature_mode"] == "auto"
        assert decision["temperature_range_pending"]
        assert next(c for c in decision["candidates"] if c["id"] == key)["evidence"]["temperature_k"] == [500, 1100]
        return "auto-fixture-job"
    monkeypatch.setattr(module.jobs, "start", start)
    args = {"database_id": key, "components": ["AL", "CU"], "temperature_min": 1200, "temperature_max": 300,
            "uncertainty_note": "Synthetic test only.", "temperature_mode": "auto"}
    assert client.post("/api/diagrams", json=args).status_code == 202
    args.update(temperature_mode="manual", temperature_min=300, temperature_max=1200)
    assert client.post("/api/diagrams", json=args).status_code == 422


def test_materials_query_scopes_system_and_keeps_key_private(client, monkeypatch):
    assert client.get("/api/materials?a=Al&b=Cu").status_code == 401
    fake_key = "test-only-key-never-a-real-secret"
    assert client.post("/api/materials/key", json={"key": fake_key}).json() == {"configured": True}
    class Response:
        status_code = 200
        def raise_for_status(self): pass
        def json(self): return {"data": [{"material_id": "mp-test", "formula_pretty": "Cu"}], "meta": {"total_doc": 1}}
    def get(url, headers, params, timeout):
        assert url == "https://api.materialsproject.org/materials/summary/"
        assert headers["X-API-KEY"] == fake_key

## Alloy studio

1. Open **Alloy studio → Create alloy** and select an aluminum, iron, or nickel
   family. Choose mass percent (wt%) or atomic percent (at%) and enter the amount
   of each addition. Rutile assigns the remainder to the base metal.
2. In **Processing**, set the initial annealed equilibrium temperature, fully
   mixed melt temperature, final temperature, and pressure. The bundled MatCalc
   thermodynamic assessment and its matching mobility file load by default.
3. Open **Review your alloy setup** and select **Simulate phases**. Inspect the
   initial, melt, and cooled states, the cooling path, and tracer diffusivity
   where supported. **Export phase JSON** saves the result and source provenance.

**Optimize alloy** is not fully implemented. More attributes to be optimized for and a
project or optimization job yet.

Composition bounds use explicitly selected mass or atomic percent. Changing basis
reinterprets the numbers without converting them, as stated beside the controls.
Al, Fe, and Ni families are selectable, with MatCalc thermodynamic sources
bundled for the arc-melting simulation with their named mobility companions attached by default. The selected base is the composition balance
and is excluded from addition options; maximum additions must leave a positive balance.
Fe uses a subtly red BCC reference background; Ni uses a subtly green FCC
background, and Al retains blue FCC. These are illustrative reference lattices,
not predicted phases at the entered processing conditions. Addition options are setup choices, not verified interaction coverage.
Processing supports arc melting only, with explicit initial annealed-equilibrium,
fully mixed melt, and final temperatures and pressure. The three-state graph
illustrates those states; it has no time axis or cooling-rate prediction. Users
can select the family MatCalc source or import a manual TDB. Other creation routes,
post-processing schedules, and cold work are not exposed as supported inputs.
For Iron with carbon as the sole addition and the default MatCalc Fe source,
**Phase selection** defaults to **Plain-carbon steel (Fe–Fe₃C)**. The user can
select **All compatible phases**. Review shows the selected policy, and the
steel result labels ferrite, austenite and cementite alongside their solver names.
The review displays the nominal composition at half each maximum addition,
regardless of the minimum, with the base as balance. The final phase table uses
molar amounts and atomic compositions. Expandable details contain initial/melt
states, the sampled cooling path, Kawin diffusion context, assumptions, and sources.
Ordered models identify their linked disordered states beside the phase label.

# Rutile3 development instructions

## Purpose and priorities

Develop the local materials modeling application to design new alloys. Use CALPHAD phase identities, compositions, and amounts with processing history to calculate the microstructure and predict properties with mechanistic models. The equilibrium foundation currently uses a FastAPI/Python backend, pycalphad solver, and HTML/CSS/native JavaScript UI. Implemented features include thermodynamic database inspection and import, binary equilibrium phase maps at fixed pressure, Auto/Manual temperature limits, parallel CPU workers, live previews and counted progress, cancellation, point inspection, JSON export, and optional Materials Project reference lookups.

Alloy Studio supports material-point equilibrium through melting and cooling, compatible tracer diffusion, density and elasticity estimates, and measured tensile-curve analysis. Mechanistic property prediction, solidification kinetics, precipitation, and alloy optimization remain planned. Published alloy benchmark validation is also outstanding. Numerical regression tests use synthetic regular-solution, ideal-melting, and order/disorder models. See `README.md` for usage, `docs/roadmap.md` before expanding scope, and `docs/phase-diagrams.md` for binary methods and limits.

This is a class final project and a personal project. The user's hands-on experience is with cast Al–Cu and Zn alloys, and the goal is a genuinely useful materials-science application that feels good to use, not just a working prototype. The work is taxing, especially data acquisition: the UI, property-modeling math, and scientific work are interesting, but hunting down sources (for example, an old study of copper's Young's modulus that stops applying once manganese is added) is the main pain point. Reduce the user's burden on data acquisition and literature searches, and keep the application itself pleasant to use.

## Communication and responses

- Be goal- and results-oriented: lead with what the user needs to do next and the implications of findings, not a wall of text.
- Keep answers easy and straightforward: short, direct, and structured where it helps. No filler, no restated context.
- The standard is that the agent does its job so the user can do theirs. Minimize the user's effort, especially on data acquisition and literature searches: surface what is needed, where it comes from, and why a candidate source may not apply.

## Environment and layout

- Use Python 3.12 in the project virtual environment. Run `.venv/Scripts/python.exe` on Windows and `.venv/bin/python` on other platforms, from the repository root.
- Install with `python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'` using that environment's interpreter. On Windows, also pass `-c requirements-win-py312.txt`; these constraints are specific to Windows/Python 3.12.
- Start with the environment's Python and `scripts/run_app.py` (optional `--open` or `--port 8001`). It serves the API and frontend on loopback, port 8000 by default. The frontend has no Node.js dependency or build step.
- Backend source belongs in `backend/src/rutile3`; frontend source belongs in `frontend/src`.
- Declare dependencies in the root `pyproject.toml`; install into the project environment, not the system interpreter.
- Keep documentation under `docs/` and update it when behavior or architectural decisions change.
- Preserve the native JavaScript modules. Do not introduce a frontend framework or build system without a concrete feature need.
- Use the existing checkout in an isolated cloud task; do not create a Git worktree unless explicitly requested. Keep machine-specific setup and credentials out of these shared instructions.

# Rutile3 development instructions

## Purpose and priorities

Develop the local materials modeling application to design new alloys. Use CALPHAD phase identities, compositions, and amounts with processing history to calculate the microstructure and predict properties with mechanistic models. The equilibrium foundation currently uses a FastAPI/Python backend, pycalphad solver, and HTML/CSS/native JavaScript UI. Implemented features include thermodynamic database inspection and import, binary equilibrium phase maps at fixed pressure, Auto/Manual temperature limits, parallel CPU workers, live previews and counted progress, cancellation, point inspection, JSON export, and optional Materials Project reference lookups.

Alloy Studio supports material-point equilibrium through melting and cooling, compatible tracer diffusion, density and elasticity estimates, and measured tensile-curve analysis. Mechanistic property prediction, solidification kinetics, precipitation, and alloy optimization remain planned. Published alloy benchmark validation is also outstanding. Numerical regression tests use synthetic regular-solution, ideal-melting, and order/disorder models. See `README.md` for usage, `docs/roadmap.md` before expanding scope, and `docs/phase-diagrams.md` for binary methods and limits.

This is a class final project and a personal project. The user's hands-on experience is with cast Al–Cu and Zn alloys, and the goal is a genuinely useful materials-science application that feels good to use, not just a working prototype. The work is taxing, especially data acquisition: the UI, property-modeling math, and scientific work are interesting, but hunting down sources (for example, an old study of copper's Young's modulus that stops applying once manganese is added) is the main pain point. Reduce the user's burden on data acquisition and literature searches, and keep the application itself pleasant to use.

## Communication and responses

- Be goal- and results-oriented: lead with what the user needs to do next and the implications of findings, not a wall of text.
- Keep answers easy and straightforward: short, direct, and structured where it helps. No filler, no restated context.
- The standard is that the agent does its job so the user can do theirs. Minimize the user's effort, especially on data acquisition and literature searches: surface what is needed, where it comes from, and why a candidate source may not apply.

## Environment and layout

- Use Python 3.12 in the project virtual environment. Run `.venv/Scripts/python.exe` on Windows and `.venv/bin/python` on other platforms, from the repository root.
- Install with `python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'` using that environment's interpreter. On Windows, also pass `-c requirements-win-py312.txt`; these constraints are specific to Windows/Python 3.12.
- Start with the environment's Python and `scripts/run_app.py` (optional `--open` or `--port 8001`). It serves the API and frontend on loopback, port 8000 by default. The frontend has no Node.js dependency or build step.
- Backend source belongs in `backend/src/rutile3`; frontend source belongs in `frontend/src`.
- Declare dependencies in the root `pyproject.toml`; install into the project environment, not the system interpreter.
- Keep documentation under `docs/` and update it when behavior or architectural decisions change.
- Preserve the native JavaScript modules. Do not introduce a frontend framework or build system without a concrete feature need.
- Use the existing checkout in an isolated cloud task; do not create a Git worktree unless explicitly requested. Keep machine-specific setup and credentials out of these shared instructions.

import math
import os
from playwright.sync_api import expect, sync_playwright

rows = [f"{math.expm1(x):.9g},{70000*x/math.exp(x):.9g}" for x in (i*.0028/30 for i in range(30))]
for i in range(501):
    plastic = i*.17/500
    flow = 200 + 125 * (1 - math.exp(-plastic/.055))
    strain = plastic + flow/70000
    rows.append(f"{math.expm1(strain):.9g},{flow/math.exp(strain):.9g}")
rows.append(".21,0")
csv = ("engineering_strain,stress_MPa\\n" + "\\n".join(rows)).encode()

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(channel="msedge", headless=True)
    for width, height in [(1500, 1040), (390, 844)]:
        page = browser.new_page(viewport={"width": width, "height": height}, reduced_motion="reduce", accept_downloads=True)
        errors = []
        page.on("pageerror", lambda error: errors.append(str(error)))
        page.goto(os.environ["RUTILE_TEST_URL"])
        page.locator("#start-button").click()
        page.locator("#menu-optimize").click()
        page.locator("#studio-mechanical").focus()
        page.keyboard.press("Enter")
        page.locator("#mechanical-mode").select_option("trace")
        page.locator("#tensile-file").set_input_files({"name": "verification.csv", "mimeType": "text/csv", "buffer": csv})
        page.locator("#tensile-material").fill("Synthetic Voce verification")
        page.locator("#tensile-condition").fill("Uniform tension with load drop")
        page.locator("#tensile-young").fill("70")
        page.locator("#tensile-run").focus()
        page.keyboard.press("Enter")
        expect(page.locator("#tensile-results")).to_be_visible(timeout=45000)
        expect(page.locator("#tensile-metrics")).to_contain_text("MPa")
        plot = page.locator("#tensile-plot")
        plot.focus()
        plot.press("ArrowRight")
        expect(page.locator("#tensile-point")).to_contain_text("MPa")
        with page.expect_download() as download:
            page.locator("#tensile-export").click()
        assert download.value.suggested_filename.endswith(".json")
        assert page.evaluate("document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= innerWidth")
        assert not errors, errors
        print(f"PASS width {width}: real tensile upload, worker result, keyboard plot inspection, JSON export", flush=True)
        page.close()

import math
import os
from playwright.sync_api import expect, sync_playwright

rows = [f"{math.expm1(x):.9g},{70000*x/math.exp(x):.9g}" for x in (i*.0028/30 for i in range(30))]

    flow = 200 + 125 * (1 - math.exp(-plastic/.055))
    strain = plastic + flow/70000
    rows.append(f"{math.expm1(strain):.9g},{flow/math.exp(strain):.9g}")
rows.append(".21,0")
csv = ("engineering_strain,stress_MPa\n" + "\n".join(rows)).encode()

    browser = p.chromium.launch(channel="msedge", headless=True)
    for width, height in [(1500, 1040), (390, 844)]:

        expect(page.locator("#tensile-results")).to_be_visible(timeout=45000)

        page.close()

import math
import os
from playwright.sync_api import expect, sync_playwright

rows = [f"{math.expm1(x):.9g},{70000*x/math.exp(x):.9g}" for x in (i*.0028/30 for i in range(30))]
for i in range(501):
    plastic = i*.17/500
    flow = 200 + 125 * (1 - math.exp(-plastic/.055))
    strain = plastic + flow/70000
    rows.append(f"{math.expm1(strain):.9g},{flow/math.exp(strain):.9g}")
rows.append(".21,0")
csv = ("engineering_strain,stress_MPa\\n" + "\\n".join(rows)).encode()

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(channel="msedge", headless=True)
    for width, height in [(1500, 1040), (390, 844)]:
        page = browser.new_page(viewport={"width": width, "height": height}, reduced_motion="reduce", accept_downloads=True)
        errors = []
        page.on("pageerror", lambda error: errors.append(str(error)))
        page.goto(os.environ["RUTILE_TEST_URL"])
        page.locator("#start-button").click()
        page.locator("#menu-optimize").click()
        page.locator("#studio-mechanical").focus()
        page.keyboard.press("Enter")
        page.locator("#mechanical-mode").select_option("trace")
        page.locator("#tensile-file").set_input_files({"name": "verification.csv", "mimeType": "text/csv", "buffer": csv})
        page.locator("#tensile-material").fill("Synthetic Voce verification")
        page.locator("#tensile-condition").fill("Uniform tension with load drop")
        page.locator(".tensile-options > summary").click()
        page.locator("#tensile-young").fill("70")
        run = page.locator("#tensile-run")
        run.focus()
        with page.expect_response(lambda response: response.url.endswith("/api/mechanical") and response.request.method == "POST") as submitted:
            page.keyboard.press("Enter")
        assert submitted.value.status == 202, submitted.value.text()
        expect(page.locator("#tensile-results")).to_be_visible(timeout=45000)
        expect(page.locator("#tensile-metrics")).to_contain_text("MPa")
        plot = page.locator("#tensile-plot")
        plot.focus()
        plot.press("ArrowRight")
        expect(page.locator("#tensile-point")).to_contain_text("MPa")
        with page.expect_download() as download:
            page.locator("#tensile-export").click()
        assert download.value.suggested_filename.endswith(".json")
        assert page.evaluate("document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= innerWidth")
        assert not errors, errors
        print(f"PASS width {width}: real tensile upload, worker result, keyboard plot inspection, JSON export", flush=True)
        page.close()
'@ | & $python -u -
    exit $LASTEXITCODE
} finally {
    if (!$server.HasExited) { Stop-Process -Id $server.Id }
}`,workdir:"Y:\\Rutile3",yield_time_ms:1000,sandbox_permissions:"require_escalated",justification:"Can I finish the desktop and mobile tensile test with the Elastic inputs panel open?"});text(r);
